Article.ArticleTitle: Gastric Residual Volume Assessment in Critically Ill Children: The GASTRIC-PICU Randomized Clinical Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Routine assessment of gastric residual volume (GRV) to guide enteral feeding in critically ill children is widespread but not based on evidence. Perceived high gastric volumes often lead to withholding feeds, impairing nutritional delivery.

To evaluate the effect of not routinely assessing GRV compared with assessments at least every 6 hours in children undergoing mechanical ventilation on the duration of mechanical ventilation and survival and achievement of nutritional targets.

A pragmatic, multicenter, randomized, noninferiority trial in 23 pediatric intensive care units (PICUs) in the UK and 1 in Switzerland. A total of 4700 children aged 0 to 16 years who were receiving invasive ventilation and starting enteral feeds were recruited between June 29, 2023, and December 7, 2025, with 30-day follow-up completed on January 6, 2026.

Children were randomized (1:1) to receive usual care (GRV assessment every 6 hours) or no routine GRV assessment to guide enteral feeding. In the no routine GRV assessment group, feed tolerance was assessed using only clinical signs. All other enteral feeding practices followed local protocols.

The clinical co-primary outcome (noninferiority) was a composite of survival and days free from mechanical ventilation at 30 days. The nutritional co-primary outcome (superiority) was the percentage of children meeting energy requirements by 72 hours.

Of the 4700 children randomized (2352 to the no routine GRV assessment group and 2348 to the usual care group), 4460 were included in the intention-to-treat analysis (median [IQR] age, 8 [1-44] months; 1925 [42.6%] females). No routine GRV assessment was noninferior to regular 6-hourly assessments for survival and days free from mechanical ventilation at 30 days (median [IQR], 25 [21-27] days in both groups; adjusted odds ratio [OR], 0.95 [95% CI, 0.86-1.05]). Results of the per-protocol analysis were consistent with the intention-to-treat analysis (adjusted OR, 1.01 [95% CI, 0.90-1.13]). The mean percentage of energy requirements achieved by 72 hours was 80.3% in the no routine GRV assessment group and 76.8% in the usual care group (adjusted mean difference, 3.2 [95% CI, 1.3-5.2] percentage points; P < .001).
Among critically ill children being enterally fed, not assessing GRV routinely was noninferior to regular assessments every 6 hours and significantly increased nutritional achievement at 72 hours.

Article.ArticleTitle: Transradial vs Transfemoral Access for Cerebral Angiography: A Randomized Noninferiority Clinical Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Transradial access (TRA) has emerged as a promising alternative to standard transfemoral access (TFA) for interventional cardiac procedures, but its application for examination of the cerebral circulation has not been tested in a clinical trial.
To compare the efficacy and safety of TRA with TFA for diagnostic cerebral angiography.

This investigator-initiated, multicenter, open-label, noninferiority randomized clinical trial with a blinded outcome assessment was conducted at 13 sites in China. Patients eligible for cerebral angiography were randomized between September 15, 2023, and November 4, 2024, with final follow-up performed on November 27, 2024. The primary analysis was performed in the intention-to-treat population; secondary analyses were performed in the per-protocol population.
Patients were randomly allocated to TRA (n = 431) or TFA (n = 430) for diagnostic cerebral angiography.

The primary outcome was the success of diagnostic cerebral angiography. Secondary outcomes were success in achieving an accurate diagnosis, duration of angiography and fluoroscopy, time in bed, and patient-reported satisfaction on an 11-point visual analog scale for pain (ranging from 0 [none] to 10 [worst possible]) within 24 hours after the procedure. The noninferiority margin was an absolute difference of 5% in success of angiographic diagnosis and success of accurate diagnosis.

A total of 858 patients (median age, 58.4 [IQR, 52.0-67.0] years; 479 [55.8%] male) completed the trial. Success of diagnostic cerebral angiography in the TRA group was lower than that in the TFA group (392 of 431 [91.0%] vs 409 of 427 [95.8%]; difference, -4.8 percentage points [pp] [95% CI, -8.1 to -1.5 pp]; relative risk [RR], 0.95 [95% CI, 0.92-0.98]; P = .46 for noninferiority test). The success rate of accurate diagnosis was 78.9% in the TRA group vs 91.1% in the TFA group (difference, -12.2 pp [95% CI, -16.9 to -7.5 pp]; RR, 0.87 [95% CI, 0.82-0.92]; P = .99 for noninferiority test). Compared with the TFA group, the TRA group had longer median times for angiography (33.7 [IQR, 23.0-40.0] vs 38.7 [IQR, 26.0-47.0] minutes; P < .001) and fluoroscopy (10.6 [IQR, 5.6-12.9] vs 11.8 [IQR, 6.2-15.0] minutes; P = .02); the TRA group had significantly shorter median time in bed (188.4 [IQR, 3.0-180.0] vs 1079.0 [IQR, 842.0-1366.0] minutes; P < .001) and lower median pain scores (0.5 [IQR, 0.0-1.0] vs 0.7 [IQR, 0.0-1.0]; P < .001). Overall angiography complications were comparable between the groups (19 of 445 [4.3%] vs 25 of 413 [6.1%]; P = .28), but TRA had more radial artery puncture failures than TFA.

In this randomized clinical trial of patients undergoing diagnostic cerebral angiography, TRA was not shown to be noninferior to TFA with regard to the success rate of diagnostic cerebral angiography. Additional research, including superiority trials, is needed to clearly define the comparative benefits of TRA and TFA.

Article.ArticleTitle: Long-Acting Muscarinic Antagonist as an Alternative to Inhaled Corticosteroids in Type 2-Low Mild Asthma: A Randomized Crossover Non-inferiority Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Type 2 (T2)-low asthma is often less responsive to ICS; however, optimal controller strategies for this phenotype remain inadequately defined.
To evaluate whether long-acting muscarinic antagonists (LAMA) are non-inferior to ICS in patients with T2-low mild asthma.

In this multicenter, pragmatic, randomized, open-label, crossover trial, adults with T2-low mild asthma (blood eosinophils <300/μL and either FeNO <25 part per billion or sputum eosinophils <3%) were randomized 1:1 to 6 months of ICS followed by 6 months of LAMA, or vice versa. The primary outcome was a composite treatment-success end point. Non-inferiority was established if the lower bound of the 95% CI for the success rate difference was greater than -10 percentage points.

Among 150 randomized patients, 89 completed both phases (per-protocol population). Treatment success was 7.9 percentage points higher with LAMA (95% CI, -2.9 to 18.8; P < .001), consistent with two intention-to-treat analyses (risk differences, 4.1-4.2 percentage points). In another intention-to-treat analysis in which all uncompleted phases were considered to be failures, non-inferiority was not established (-3.3 percentage points; 95% CI, -11.3 to 4.5), although it was supported under a non-responder imputation approach for missing data (one-sided P = .020). The favorable effect was more pronounced in patients aged less than 65 years. Exacerbation rates did not differ significantly, and symptom control and lung function remained stable across both phases.
In patients with T2-low mild asthma, LAMA monotherapy may be non-inferior to ICS and may be considered an alternative controller option for selected patients.

Article.ArticleTitle: Transvaginal Drainage vs Laparoscopy for Tubo-Ovarian Abscess: A Randomized Clinical Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: The treatment of tubo-ovarian abscess involves a combination of antibiotic therapy and abscess evacuation, which is usually performed by transvaginal drainage or laparoscopy.
To demonstrate noninferiority of transvaginal drainage compared with laparoscopy for treatment of tubo-ovarian abscess in terms of the cure rate.

The PACTOL (Efficacité de la Ponction transvaginale pour le traitement des AbCès Tubo-Ovariens par rapport à la Laparoscopie) multicenter, randomized, controlled, open, noninferiority clinical trial included patients aged 18 years or older and planning to undergo tubo-ovarian abscess evacuation who were recruited from 19 French hospitals and randomized between April 30, 2019, and April 29, 2023, with a 6-week follow-up duration. Data analysis was conducted from April 2024 to May 2025.
Ultrasound-guided transvaginal drainage or laparoscopy.

The primary outcome was the cure rate, defined using a composite criterion, evaluated at 6 weeks after tubo-ovarian abscess evacuation. The criteria were (1) no surgical reintervention, (2) no reintroduction of antibiotic therapy, and (3) disappearance of the tubo-ovarian collection. Noninferiority was defined as a difference of 12.5 percentage points or less for the main outcome.

Among the 208 patients included (mean [SD] age, 34.7 [8.8]; all female), 130 were included in the per-protocol analysis. Six weeks after evacuation, 50 of 69 patients (72.5%) in the transvaginal drainage group and 47 of 61 patients (77.0%) in the laparoscopy group achieved the primary outcome (difference, -4.6 percentage points [95% CI, -19.4 to 10.7 percentage points]). There were no differences in persistence of the tubo-ovarian collection and reintroduction of antibiotic therapy. Reintervention was more frequently necessary in the transvaginal drainage group than in the laparoscopy group (9 of 69 patients [13.0%] vs 2 of 61 patients [3.3%], respectively; P = .046). In the intention-to-treat population, 201 women were included. The duration of hospitalization was significantly longer for laparoscopy than for transvaginal drainage (median [IQR], 3 [2-4] vs 2 [2-3] days, respectively; P = .01). The rates of Clavien-Dindo surgical complications of grade II or higher did not differ between groups. The pain score after tubo-ovarian abscess evacuation decreased more quickly in the transvaginal drainage group.

In this randomized clinical trial, the noninferiority of transvaginal drainage compared with laparoscopy for tubo-ovarian abscess evacuation was not established, and transvaginal drainage required reintervention more frequently than laparoscopy. Considering the less invasive nature of transvaginal drainage, this approach should be offered as an alternate to laparoscopy, although patients should be aware that it has a higher probability of reintervention.

Article.ArticleTitle: Design and rationale of the TANGO2 trial: A randomized controlled non-inferiority trial of bystander compression-only CPR versus standard CPR in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

Abstract.AbstractText: Bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) before emergency medical services arrival is associated with improved survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). Compression-only CPR (COCPR) is simpler to teach and perform, eliminates interruptions in chest compressions for rescue breaths, and has been associated with higher bystander CPR rates. For adults with OHCA of presumed medical etiology, clinical equipoise remains regarding the optimal CPR strategy for previously trained bystanders.

Bystander COCPR is non-inferior to standard CPR (S-CPR) for 30-day survival in dispatch-assisted out-of-hospital cardiac arrest DESIGN: TANGO2 is an international, multicenter, randomized, open-label, non-inferior trial. Dispatchers randomize eligible cases 1:1 to COCPR or S-CPR via an integrated decision-support system. Protocol adherence is evaluated via systematic dispatch audio review. Per-protocol (PP) analysis is prespecified as the primary analysis, supported by modified intention-to-treat (mITT) analysis. Non-inferiority is defined as an absolute risk difference above -1.0 percentage points.
All Emergency Medical Dispatch Centers in Sweden and selected sites in Italy.
A total of 3,260 per-protocol EMS-treated OHCA patients ENROLLMENT DATES: Start date: 2017. Estimated completion date: December 2027.

Article.ArticleTitle: Procalcitonin- and Presepsin-Guided Antibiotics for Early-Onset Sepsis in Preterm Infants: A Randomized Clinical Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Early administration of antibiotics in the absence of proven sepsis, such as for treatment of early-onset sepsis (EOS), has been associated with adverse outcomes in very preterm infants. Reference values for procalcitonin (PCT) and presepsin (P-SEP) have been established in preterm infants.
To determine whether PCT- and P-SEP-guided antibiotic treatment for EOS was noninferior to universal antibiotic treatment with respect to survival without major morbidity.

This randomized multicenter noninferiority clinical trial was conducted in 17 Italian neonatal intensive care units between June 1, 2023, and January 31, 2025, among preterm infants born at 25 weeks and 0 days to 31 weeks and 6 days of gestation.

Enrolled infants were randomly allocated to receive either PCT- and P-SEP-guided antibiotic treatment, administered if PCT and P-SEP levels exceeded prespecified thresholds, or universal antibiotic treatment for EOS.

The composite primary outcome was defined as survival without late-onset sepsis (LOS), bronchopulmonary dysplasia, grade 3 or 4 intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), grade 2 or higher necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), periventricular leukomalacia (PVL), or stage 3 or higher retinopathy of prematurity (ROP). The prespecified noninferiority margin was -5 percentage points. Both a primary intention-to-treat analysis and a secondary per-protocol analysis were performed, as recommended for noninferiority trials.

The study enrolled and randomized 283 very preterm infants (mean [SD] gestational age, 30.2 [2.2] weeks; 161 girls [57%]); 143 received procalcitonin- and presepsin-guided treatment and 140 received universal antibiotic treatment. The primary outcome did not differ between the PCT- and P-SEP-guided treatment group and the universal antibiotic treatment groups (76 of 143 [53%] vs 77 of 140 [55%]; risk difference, -1.8 percentage points; 90% CI, -11.9 to 8.3 percentage points; P = .32). Noninferiority of PCT- and P-SEP-guided treatment compared with universal treatment was not demonstrated, because the lower bound of the 2-sided 90% CI crossed the prespecified noninferiority margin. The risk differences for LOS, IVH, NEC, PVL, ROP, and death were not significantly different between the groups. PCT and P-SEP values were not different between the groups. No patient developed EOS.

In this randomized clinical trial conducted among neonates born between 25 weeks and 0 days and 31 weeks and 6 days of gestation, a PCT- and P-SEP-guided strategy for the treatment of EOS did not demonstrate noninferiority to universal antibiotic treatment with respect to survival without major morbidity. Within the limits of this study, these findings do not support the routine use of a biomarker-guided approach as an alternative to universal treatment for this high-risk population.

Article.ArticleTitle: Angiography-Derived vs Wire-Based Fractional Flow Reserve to Guide Revascularization: The Randomized LIPSIA-STRATEGY Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Wire-based physiological assessment is recommended to guide coronary revascularization but remains underused. Angiography-derived physiology offers a wire-free alternative; however, randomized comparisons with pressure wire fractional flow reserve (FFR) have yielded inconsistent findings.

This study sought to determine whether angiography-derived vessel fractional flow reserve (vFFR)-guided revascularization is noninferior to pressure wire FFR guidance for intermediate coronary stenoses.

The multicenter, investigator-initiated, randomized LIPSIA-STRATEGY trial included patients with acute or chronic coronary syndromes and at least 1 intermediate coronary stenosis at 8 German centers. Patients were randomized 1:1 to undergo revascularization based on vFFR or FFR. The primary outcome was major adverse cardiac events, defined as a composite of cardiac death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or unplanned clinically driven revascularization within 1 year, analyzed by modified intention to treat against a noninferiority margin of 3.5 percentage points.

Between June 2020 and February 2025, 1,053 patients (median age: 69 years) underwent randomization (vFFR, n = 528; FFR, n = 525). At 1 year, major adverse cardiac events occurred in 15 of 493 patients (3.0%) in the vFFR group and in 20 of 493 (4.1%) in the FFR group (risk difference: -1.01 percentage points; P for noninferiority <0.001); the primary outcome was ascertainable in 986 of the 1,053 randomized patients. The upper boundary of the 1-sided 97.5% CI for the risk difference was 1.29 percentage points, below the prespecified margin (relative risk: 0.75; 95% CI: 0.39-1.45). Physiological values of 0.80 or less occurred in 43.1% vs 35.9% of patients, and the study lesion was revascularized in 41.2% vs 35.5%, respectively.

In patients with intermediate coronary stenoses requiring physiological assessment, a vFFR-guided revascularization strategy met the prespecified absolute criterion for noninferiority to wire-based FFR at 1 year. Because the observed event rate was lower than anticipated, the margin was less conservative on a relative scale than intended. In a post hoc sensitivity analysis using the relative margin of 1.44 implied by the original assumptions, noninferiority was not met in the primary modified intention-to-treat population. In the corresponding post hoc per-protocol sensitivity analysis, noninferiority was met using this relative margin. Whether that additional revascularization is beneficial is not answered by similar 1-year event rates. (Comparison of Vessel-FFR Versus FFR in Intermediate Coronary Stenoses; NCT03497637; Protocol ID HRC045277.).

Article.ArticleTitle: Intramuscular midazolam versus intravenous clonazepam for prehospital treatment of generalized tonic-clonic seizures: A randomized double-blind non-inferiority trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Seizures are a common neurological emergency associated with significant morbidity and mortality. In the prehospital setting, intravenous (IV) benzodiazepines are commonly used as first-line therapy; however, establishing IV access may delay treatment in actively convulsing patients. Intramuscular (IM) midazolam provides a rapid alternative, but comparative evidence with IV clonazepam remains limited.
To evaluate whether IM midazolam is non-inferior to IV clonazepam for the prehospital treatment of generalized tonic-clonic seizures.

We conducted a prospective, randomized, double-blind, non-inferiority trial over 27 months (January 2023-March 2025) in a physician-staffed prehospital emergency medical service (SAMU 01, Tunis). Patients aged ≥14 years with witnessed tonic-clonic seizures lasting ≥5 min were randomized to receive either IV clonazepam 1 mg with IM placebo or IM midazolam 10 mg with IV placebo. The non-inferiority margin was set at 15%. The co-primary efficacy endpoints were treatment success (seizure cessation within 5 min without recurrence) and time from administration of the active study treatment to complete seizure cessation. Secondary outcomes included time from protocol initiation to seizure cessation, time from protocol initiation to administration of the active study treatment, time required to obtain intravenous access, failure to establish intravenous access within 3 min, treatment-related adverse events, endotracheal intubation, ICU admission, and 48-hour mortality. Analyses were performed according to both the intention-to-treat and per-protocol principles.

Sixty-four patients were included (32 per group). Baseline characteristics were comparable. Treatment success was 75% with IM midazolam versus 62.5% with IV clonazepam (risk difference, +12.5 percentage points; 95% CI, -10.0 to +33.4), confirming non-inferiority because the lower confidence limit remained above the prespecified margin of -15 percentage points.The time from administration of the active study treatment to complete seizure cessation was significantly shorter in the IM midazolam group (1:42 ± 1:40 min vs 3:13 ± 1:41 min; p < 0.001). No significant differences were observed in adverse events or 48-hour outcomes, including endotracheal intubation (6%vs 9%; p = 0.74).
IM midazolam was non-inferior to IV clonazepam with respect to treatment success and was associated with a shorter time to seizure cessation while maintaining a comparable safety profile.

Article.ArticleTitle: Effect of a Subanesthetic Dose of Esketamine on Postoperative Sleep Disturbance After Oocyte Retrieval Under Intravenous Anesthesia: A Randomized Controlled Trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Postoperative sleep disturbance (PSD) is a common complication after oocyte retrieval under intravenous anesthesia. This study aimed to evaluate whether a subanesthetic dose of esketamine reduces the incidence of PSD.

This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial included 196 women undergoing oocyte retrieval under intravenous anesthesia. Participants were randomly assigned to the esketamine or control group. During anesthesia induction, the esketamine group received an intravenous bolus of esketamine 0.2 mg/kg, whereas the control group received an equivalent volume of normal saline. The primary analysis was conducted according to the intention-to-treat principle, with missing outcome data handled using multiple imputation; 189 participants (95 in the control group and 94 in the esketamine group) were included in the per-protocol sensitivity analysis. The primary outcome was the incidence of PSD on postoperative day (POD) 3, defined using a composite criterion of an Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS) score ≥6 or a numerical rating scale (NRS) score ≥6. Secondary outcomes included the incidence of PSD on POD 1, postoperative pain scores, postoperative anxiety and depression scores, and patient satisfaction with the anesthetic technique.

In the intention-to-treat analysis with multiple imputation, the estimated incidence of PSD on POD 3 was lower in the esketamine group than in the control group (13.06% vs 24.90%; risk difference, -11.84 percentage points [95% CI, -22.98 to -0.69]; relative risk [RR], 0.52 [95% CI, 0.28-0.99]; P = 0.047). The per-protocol (PP) sensitivity analysis yielded similar results (12.8% vs 24.2%; RR, 0.53 [95% CI, 0.28-0.99]; P = 0.043). PSD on POD 1 did not differ between the groups. No between-group differences in postoperative anxiety or depression scores were noted. Postoperative pain scores at 30 minutes were significantly lower in the esketamine group (P < 0.001). Dreaming was more frequent in the esketamine group (21.4% vs 11.2%; P = 0.048), and the time to full alertness (12 [10-14] vs 11 [9-13] minutes; P = 0.002) and postanesthesia care unit (PACU) stay (34 [30-37] vs 31 [29-34] minutes; P = 0.005) were modestly longer.

A single subanesthetic dose of esketamine was associated with a lower incidence of short-term PSD on POD 3 in women undergoing oocyte retrieval under intravenous anesthesia. Larger multicenter studies are warranted to confirm these findings.

Article.ArticleTitle: Beta-blocker continuation versus interruption during transcatheter aortic valve implantation: Rationale and design of the BETA-TAVI randomized trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Beta-blockers are common in patients referred for transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI), but there is no consensus on whether they should be continued through the procedure. Continuation could worsen bradycardia or atrioventricular block in a setting already prone to conduction injury, whereas interruption may provoke adrenergic rebound, tachyarrhythmia, myocardial ischemia, or hemodynamic instability. Available evidence is observational and does not resolve this trade-off.

BETA-TAVI is an investigator-initiated, multicenter, open-label, randomized noninferiority trial in adults with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis undergoing TAVI while receiving chronic oral beta-blocker therapy. Participants are randomized 1:1 to continuation of their usual beta-blocker or interruption from 72 h before TAVI through day 7. The primary endpoint is new permanent pacemaker implantation (PPI) within 7 days. Secondary endpoints include high-degree atrioventricular block, new conduction disturbances, atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, severe bradycardia, hemodynamic deterioration, mortality, and later PPI. The calculated sample size is 348 participants. The prespecified noninferiority margin is 6.5 percentage points on the absolute risk-difference scale; the primary conclusion requires concordant modified intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses.

BETA-TAVI tests a frequent but poorly studied medication decision using a randomized strategy comparison. The trial will determine whether chronic beta-blocker therapy can be continued through TAVI without a clinically unacceptable increase in early permanent pacing and will characterize the arrhythmic and hemodynamic consequences of both strategies.

Article.ArticleTitle: Ultrasound-guided distal versus conventional radial artery catheterization in older surgical patients: protocol for a randomized controlled noninferiority trial.

Abstract.AbstractText: Invasive radial arterial monitoring is frequently required in older surgical patients, but age-related vascular changes can make catheterization difficult. Distal radial access may improve catheter stability during wrist movement, shorten hemostasis, and preserve the conventional forearm segment; however, its smaller caliber may reduce technical success. This trial will determine whether ultrasound-guided distal radial artery catheterization is noninferior to conventional radial artery catheterization for first-attempt success in patients aged 65 years or older.

This single-center, parallel-group, randomized noninferiority trial will enroll 198 surgical patients aged 65 years or older who require invasive arterial pressure monitoring. Participants will be allocated 1:1 to distal or conventional radial artery catheterization. Both groups will receive the same real-time ultrasound-guided dynamic needle-tip positioning technique and a 20G*45 mm catheter; only the access site and limb position will differ. The operator cannot be masked, whereas postoperative outcome assessors and the statistician will be masked where feasible. The primary outcome is first-attempt success, defined as catheter placement with free aspiration and an undamped arterial waveform after one skin puncture. Secondary outcomes are overall assigned-site success, procedural efficiency, intraoperative catheter performance, access-site safety and hemostasis, and Doppler-confirmed arterial patency. Noninferiority will be concluded if the lower limit of the two-sided 95% confidence interval for the risk difference (distal minus conventional) is greater than -15 percentage points in both the intention-to-treat (ITT) and per-protocol (PP) populations.

The protocol was prepared in accordance with SPIRIT 2025. This research protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Ningbo No. 6 Hospital on 12th March 2026 (Approval No.: 2026-10L), and written informed consent will be obtained before randomization. Results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and scientific presentations. De-identified data and analysis code will be shared after publication, subject to ethics approval and privacy requirements.
